subject: need to explain 'anova' like if I were a 5-year-old

messages.author: c3997138dbab4a1f
messages.subject: need to explain 'anova' like if I were a 5-year-old
parts:
My head spins around (sometimes) when I use an anova function to compare models. 
I know this is not an issue related only to mirt but since there is a mirt::anova I thought it could be useful to discuss it.

So, I am comparing two models mod.1 and mod.2, where mod.2 is a constrained version of mod.1 (i.e., mod.2 is nested within mod.1?)  
I ran the

anova(mod.1, mod.2) #by the way it is great how the order of the models is irrelevant and it gets rearranged accordingly (sweet)

this is what I get:
Model 1: mirt(data = data, model = 1, constrain = const.1)
Model 2: mirt(data = data, model = 1)

       AIC     AICc    SABIC      BIC    logLik      X2 df p
1 39127.64 39132.56 39233.74 39405.27 -19509.82             
2 38882.33 38896.30 39059.16 39345.04 -19351.16 317.318 36 0


So, mod.1 has better fit statistics... however... there is some rejection of H0. 
What is H0 of this anova test?

1) Am I rejecting that the constrains are valid? 
That is, that it is necessary to free these parameters for the model to fit the data better?
My interpretation would be that mod.1 is closer to reality than mod.2, e.g., it is better at explaining the data

2) Am I rejecting that the two models have indeed different fit?
In which case it comes down to other criteria to select which model fits better... 
if we go by the gof statistics I would say mod.1 (although sometimes, not here, AIC and BIC contradict each other :-/ )
if I think parsimony then mod.2 is a better model because it has less parameters to estimate. 

I hope my issue is clear... it seems to me a bit more complicated than adding predictors in a GLM, although sometimes those kinds of model comparisons using anova also make my head spin. 

thanks

~MRE

On Sat, Jan 11, 2014 at 3:26 PM, Manolo Romero Escobar
<emro...@gmail.com> wrote:
> My head spins around (sometimes) when I use an anova function to compare
> models.
> I know this is not an issue related only to mirt but since there is a
> mirt::anova I thought it could be useful to discuss it.
>
> So, I am comparing two models mod.1 and mod.2, where mod.2 is a constrained
> version of mod.1 (i.e., mod.2 is nested within mod.1?)
> I ran the
>
> anova(mod.1, mod.2) #by the way it is great how the order of the models is
> irrelevant and it gets rearranged accordingly (sweet)
>
> this is what I get:
> Model 1: mirt(data = data, model = 1, constrain = const.1)
> Model 2: mirt(data = data, model = 1)
>
> AIC AICc SABIC BIC logLik X2 df p
> 1 39127.64 39132.56 39233.74 39405.27 -19509.82
> 2 38882.33 38896.30 39059.16 39345.04 -19351.16 317.318 36 0
>
>
> So, mod.1 has better fit statistics... however... there is some rejection of
> H0.
> What is H0 of this anova test?

H0 is the null hypotheses that the two values are equally likely,
i.e., have the same height in the log-likelihood function given their
parameters. If the models are equally likely, but one uses more
parameters, then usually for parsimony reasons you wouldn't want to
use the more complicated model if it doesn't actually fit better given
your observed data. The X2 is actually a distance measure based on the
2*(log.likelihood_1 - log-likelihood_2), which measures how far apart
one likelihood is from another in terms of ML height, and as it turns
out is distributed as a chi-squared value in large samples.

>
> 1) Am I rejecting that the constrains are valid?

You reject saying that by including the extra parameters the data were
much more likely to be observed than when not including them. So they
contribute to how well you could theoretically reproduce the data
given only model parameter inputs.

> That is, that it is necessary to free these parameters for the model to fit
> the data better?
> My interpretation would be that mod.1 is closer to reality than mod.2, e.g.,
> it is better at explaining the data
>
> 2) Am I rejecting that the two models have indeed different fit?
> In which case it comes down to other criteria to select which model fits
> better...
> if we go by the gof statistics I would say mod.1 (although sometimes, not
> here, AIC and BIC contradict each other :-/ )
> if I think parsimony then mod.2 is a better model because it has less
> parameters to estimate.

This is a pretty debatable issue, and depends more on what the models
are being used for. You're right, AIC and BIC often differ since BIC
gives a larger penalty to smaller sample sizes than AIC. I think one
is just more conservative than the other really. Personally, if I see
the BIC lower than I'm extremely confident that the inclusion of the
extra parameters is important.

Adding parameters of course always makes the observed data easier to
reproduce, and hence decreases the log-likelihood, but you really need
to be careful since adding too many parameters actually negatively
affects the precision of all the estimated parameters.....so these
information stats try to provide a good point at which you should stop
looking for extra pars and start looking at the parameter standard
errors. Cheers.

Phil
